proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(I\in\mathfrak J_2^{\mathrm{nw}}\).  By \(\text{def:no-width-input-class}\), the graph is finite and acyclic, every exogenous root has at most two observed children, all response coordinates and all raw equality rows are explicitly present, the observational table is compatible, and the query is block-affine.  Delete singleton-valued observed arguments from the response tables; this changes neither a response-table set nor an equality row.

We first bound the exact raw rank of an original block.  Suppose that \(c\) has two nontrivial children.  For \(j\in\{1,2\}\), let \(d_j\) be the number of nontrivial binary observed arguments of the \(j\)-th child's response function and set \(h_j=2^{d_j}\).  There are \(2^{h_j}\) deterministic binary response functions for that child, so completeness of the response list gives
\[
N_c:=|R_c|=2^{h_1+h_2}. \tag{1}
\]
There are at most \(2^{d_1+d_2}=h_1h_2\) joint external-parent contexts.  Sharing an observed parent, or having an observed edge between the two children, can only reduce this number because an internal child value is then not a freely chosen external context coordinate.  At a fixed context a deterministic response tuple produces exactly one of at most four joint binary child outputs.  Hence the corresponding raw equality rows partition \(R_c\) into at most four supports, and the total number of raw rows is at most \(4h_1h_2\).  Rank is at most the number of rows, and therefore
\[
r_c:=\operatorname{rank}(A_c)
 \le 4h_1h_2
 \le (h_1+h_2)^2
 = (\log_2N_c)^2, \tag{2}
\]
where the middle inequality is equivalent to \((h_1-h_2)^2\ge0\).

If \(c\) has one nontrivial child with \(d\) nontrivial binary observed arguments, put \(h=2^d\).  Then \(N_c=2^h\), there are at most \(h\) external contexts, and each has two output rows.  Thus
\[
r_c\le2h=2\log_2N_c. \tag{3}
\]
A block with no nontrivial child has constant dimension and rank.  Combining the cases yields the uniform bound
\[
r_c\le4(1+\log_2N_c)^2. \tag{4}
\]

For later use define
\[
L_c:=\sum_{j=0}^{r_c}\binom{N_c}{j}. \tag{5}
\]
The \(K_c\) clause of \(\text{lem:rational-factor-vertices}\) says that a point of \(K_c\) is a vertex exactly when the columns of \(A_c\) indexed by its positive support are linearly independent.  Consequently its positive support has size at most \(r_c\).  Testing every support of size at most \(r_c\), solving the associated rational system exactly, retaining precisely the nonnegative feasible solutions, and removing exact duplicates therefore produces the complete list \(\operatorname{ext}(K_c)\).  Exact Gaussian elimination and rational comparison take polynomial bit time per tested support because the full system is part of \(I\).  The same lemma gives \(O(B^2)\)-bit numerators and denominators for every retained coordinate.  Thus this list is generated in \(L_c\operatorname{poly}(B)\) bit operations.  Moreover,
\[
L_c
 \le (N_c+1)^{r_c+1}
 \le B^{O((1+\log B)^2)}, \tag{6}
\]
because \(\text{ass:complete-response-list}\) charges at least one input bit to each of the \(N_c\) response records, whence \(N_c\le B\), and (4) applies.

Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq C\) be the set of blocks occurring in at least one monomial scope of \(g\); by definition \(|\mathcal D|=\ell\).  Fix for the moment one block \(c_*\in\mathcal D\).  Generate the complete vertex list just described for every \(c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}\), and do not generate a support list for \(c_*\).  For a tuple
\[
v_{- *}\in
 \prod_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}
       \operatorname{ext}(K_c), \tag{7}
\]
block-affinity from \(\text{ass:block-affine-query}\) gives an explicitly computable rational affine function
\[
x\longmapsto g(v_{-*},x)=\alpha_{v_{-*}}+p_{v_{-*}}^{\mathsf T}x,
\qquad x\in K_{c_*}. \tag{8}
\]
There are at most \(B\) serialized monomials and at most \(B\) factors in each, and all substituted vertex coordinates have \(O(B^2)\)-bit encodings.  Hence the coefficients in (8) have encoding length polynomial in \(B\).

By \(\text{lem:rational-h-representations}\), \(K_{c_*}\) is a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron with an explicit encoding of length at most \(B\).  Apply \(\text{lem:exact-rational-linear-programming}\) to minimize or maximize (8) exactly.  If a basic optimizer is desired, first compute the optimal value, intersect \(K_{c_*}\) with the resulting rational optimal-face equality, and then lexicographically maximize the \(N_{c_*}\) coordinates by at most \(N_{c_*}\le B\) further exact linear programs.  The final point is unique: two distinct survivors would differ first in some coordinate, contradicting maximization at that lexicographic stage.  A unique point of a face is a vertex of that face and hence a vertex of \(K_{c_*}\).  The \(K_c\) clause of \(\text{lem:rational-factor-vertices}\) then shows that this basic optimizer is rational with \(O(B^2)\)-bit coordinates.  Thus each inner optimization in (8) costs \(\operatorname{poly}(B)\) bit operations.

It remains to prove that these finitely many linear programs return the global endpoints, rather than merely candidates.  By \(\text{lem:rational-h-representations}\), every \(K_c\) is compact, so the finite product is compact; the polynomial \(g\) is continuous, so its minimum and maximum are attained.  Starting from a maximizer, hold every other block fixed and apply the preceding exact linear optimization argument to one block in \(\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}\).  Replacing that block by a vertex optimizer cannot decrease the value.  Repeating over all such blocks leaves a global maximizer whose listed blocks lie in (7).  The final maximization over \(K_{c_*}\) is exactly (8).  The same argument with minimization cannot increase the value.  Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{z\in\prod_{c\in C}K_c}g(z)
 &=\max_{v_{-*}\text{ satisfying }(7)}
     \max_{x\in K_{c_*}}g(v_{-*},x),\\
\min_{z\in\prod_{c\in C}K_c}g(z)
 &=\min_{v_{-*}\text{ satisfying }(7)}
     \min_{x\in K_{c_*}}g(v_{-*},x).
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Blocks outside \(\mathcal D\) do not occur in \(g\).  For each such block, apply \(\text{lem:exact-rational-linear-programming}\) to the zero objective over its nonempty rational polyhedron and use the same lexicographic refinement to obtain one rational basic feasible point.  There are at most \(B\) blocks, so all these feasibility completions together cost \(\operatorname{poly}(B)\); no support of an irrelevant block is enumerated.

For a fixed \(c_*\), support generation costs
\(\sum_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}L_c\operatorname{poly}(B)\), while (9) invokes, for either endpoint, exactly
\[
E_{c_*}:=
\prod_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}
 |\operatorname{ext}(K_c)| \tag{10}
\]
outer rational linear programs.  Exact evaluation, comparison, and backpointer storage for each tuple have polynomial bit cost because all intermediate rational encodings are polynomial in \(B\).  The total fixed-branch bound is therefore
\[
\left(
 \sum_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}L_c+E_{c_*}
\right)\operatorname{poly}(B). \tag{11}
\]
Running the \(\ell\) choices of omitted block in round-robin and stopping when the first correct branch completes multiplies the least bound in (11) by at most \(\ell\le B\); this proves the stated minimum instance bound up to its polynomial factor.  Alternatively, for the uniform advertised rate choose \(c_*\) with largest \(L_c\).  Since every \(L_c\ge1\) and \(|\operatorname{ext}(K_c)|\le L_c\), equations (6), (10), and (11) give
\[
\left(
 \sum_{c\ne c_*}L_c+E_{c_*}
\right)\operatorname{poly}(B)
 \le
B^{O((\ell-1)(1+\log B)^2)}\operatorname{poly}(B). \tag{12}
\]
When \(\ell=1\), both the sum and the product over \(\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}\) are respectively zero and one.  Thus no relevant-block support is enumerated, (8) is a single rational linear program for each endpoint, and the complete procedure is polynomial-time.

Finally, combine an optimizing relevant tuple from (9) with the rational feasible points selected for the irrelevant blocks.  This produces rational points of \(\prod_{c\in C}K_c\) attaining both extrema.  By \(\text{prop:canonical-semantics}\), those extrema equal \(\underline\theta\) and \(\overline\theta\), and each concatenated feasible point induces a normalized finite independent-root SCM compatible with \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\) and having the same interventional query value.  Hence both sharp endpoints are exact, rationally attained, and computed without a width assumption or an implicit response-column oracle.

added_lemmas.statement: Given a rational matrix \(D\), rational vectors \(d,p\), and their binary encoding, linear-program feasibility and the finite optimum of \(p^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(\{x:Dx\le d\}\) can be computed exactly in a number of bit operations polynomial in the encoding length; in the nonempty bounded case the computation returns a rational optimal point.

attestation.note: Stable DOI supplied for the classical bit-complexity result; the proof uses only exact rational optimization in the nonempty bounded case.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
For every \(I\in\mathfrak J_2^{\mathrm{nw}}\), let \(\mathcal D\subseteq C\) be the set of the \(\ell\ge1\) original response blocks occurring in \(g\), and for \(c\in\mathcal D\) put \(N_c=|R_c|\), \(r_c=\operatorname{rank}(A_c)\), and \(L_c=\sum_{j=0}^{r_c}\binom{N_c}{j}\). If every nontrivial variable in \(V\) is binary, then the exact sharp endpoints \(\underline\theta,\overline\theta\) and rational attaining finite SCMs are computable without a width assumption. For any omitted block \(c_*\in\mathcal D\), one complete algorithm enumerates the vertex lists only for \(c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}\) and, for each resulting tuple, solves one bounded rational linear program over \(K_{c_*}\) for either endpoint. Its bit complexity is
\[
\left(
 \sum_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}L_c
 +\prod_{c\in\mathcal D\setminus\{c_*\}}
       |\operatorname{ext}(K_c)|
\right)\operatorname{poly}(B),
\]
and the product in this display is exactly the number of outer linear programs for either endpoint. Dovetailing the choices of \(c_*\) attains the minimum of the displayed instance bounds up to a polynomial factor. In particular, choosing \(c_*\) with largest \(L_c\) gives
\[
B^{O((\ell-1)(1+\log B)^2)}\operatorname{poly}(B),
\]
so \(\ell=1\) is an exact polynomial-time case. Every query-irrelevant block is completed by rational linear-program feasibility rather than support enumeration.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The active directive requires replacing the valid but coarse all-block enumeration bound by the proved all-but-one-block enumeration bound. The product of actual vertex counts is the exact outer LP count; the additive support-candidate term is retained because the frozen core proves exhaustive rank-bounded support generation, not an output-polynomial vertex enumerator. This exposes the polynomial-time one-relevant-block elbow without overstating the instance-sensitive total runtime.

proposed.justification: This gives an exact second regime when no useful width decomposition is available: one relevant block is optimized directly rather than enumerated, and a single relevant block is polynomial-time.
proposed.gap: Arroyo et al. use column generation for one intervention under a different representation; this result instead gives a fully expanded exact algorithm for several relevant canonical blocks, with complete support generation for only all but one block and an exact rational LP elbow.
proposed.consumer: A canonical optimizer can dispatch sparse-block binary queries even when measured scalar response width is large, using direct exact LP optimization for the omitted block.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The sharper proof uses the classical exact rational LP theorem and the statement must expose the support-generation term, outer vertex-tuple count, and the one-block elbow. Omitting the additive support-generation term would silently assume an output-polynomial vertex-enumeration result not present in the frozen core.

prose_updates.tldr: For the headline subcase \(\mathfrak I_{q,k}^{\ge3}\) of the cardinality-unrestricted superclass \(\mathfrak J_{q,k}\), raw observational rows bound every original response block by \(q^2(k+1)\) coordinates. Every local and equality-factor feasible set is first posed in a finite-dimensional real space by an explicit rational H-representation; separate lemmas establish boundedness, compactness, rational extreme points, and \(O(B^2)\) coordinate encoding before support enumeration. Connected equality splitting preserves width and block-affinity, so standard min-sum and max-sum elimination computes exact sharp multi-intervention endpoints, rational attaining SCMs, and skeptical replay certificates in \(2^{O(q^2(k+1)^2)}\operatorname{poly}(B)\) bit operations. Independently of width, a binary query involving \(\ell\ge1\) original response blocks is solved by enumerating complete vertex lists for only \(\ell-1\) blocks and optimizing the last block by exact rational linear programming, giving \(B^{O((\ell-1)(1+\log B)^2)}\operatorname{poly}(B)\) bit operations and a polynomial-time elbow at \(\ell=1\). The genuine open step is executable serialized refinement with universal compatible-SCM validity and endpoint realization.

project_justification.gap: Higher-degree quasi-Markovian causal bounds are addressed by stationary-point search or general epsilon-sharp polynomial optimization. Their broad admissible program classes strictly contain the semantic image of the present explicit rational bounded-width class, but neither source gives exact endpoint and skeptical-certificate guarantees on that common image. Existing column-generation work also does not supply the fully expanded, several-relevant-block exact guarantee or its one-block rational-LP elbow.
project_justification.niche: Small discrete multi-intervention queries often already materialize response columns and raw equalities, so their scalar interaction graph can be narrow even though the causal graph, objective degree, or canonical latent cardinality alone gives no tractability guarantee. When that measured width is large, a binary query may still involve only a few original response blocks.
project_justification.fill: The project supplies explicit rational H-representations in real ambient spaces, proves factor boundedness and rational vertex encoding before enumeration, proves the raw clique bound and exact within-block gluing, and then derives exact bounded-width elimination and an abstract mathematical certificate theorem. Its secondary no-width algorithm enumerates complete supports for only all but one relevant binary block and solves the omitted block by exact rational linear programming, yielding a polynomial-time one-block elbow. A concrete serialized parser, generator, executable checker, and their end-to-end refinement proof remain open.

prose_updates.related_work: Shridharan and Iyengar motivate the problem most directly: their admissible canonical program class contains the forgetful image of \(\mathfrak I_{q,k}^{\ge3}\), while their exact linear and quadratic subfamily is incomparable with the headline class because the latter contains genuine degree-at-least-three objectives and excludes one- and two-component inputs. Their higher-degree guarantee is stationary-point convergence; the exact-width theorem strictly tightens that guarantee only on the common explicit bounded-width image. The secondary binary result is different: without assuming width, it enumerates complete vertex lists for only \(\ell-1\) query-relevant original blocks and handles the last by exact rational linear programming, becoming polynomial-time at \(\ell=1\). Duarte et al.'s discrete causal polynomial-program class strictly contains the bounded-width image because it permits broader graphs, real input tables, and unbounded scalar width; the exact-width theorem tightens epsilon-sharp output to exact rational sharpness only on the shared subclass and does not subsume their admissible class. Zaffalon, Antonucci, and Cabañas establish the quasi-Markovian credal correspondence, while Zaffalon et al. show that ordinary polytree structure does not make exact credal causal inference tractable in general. Dechter supplies the standard induced-width elimination and backpointer machinery; no new elimination rule is claimed. Sachs et al. supply response-function matrices and tight symbolic certificates for a linear class, and Li, Passmore, and Paulson supply the skeptical producer--checker architecture. Arroyo et al. address response-state explosion through single-intervention column generation under a different representation; the present secondary result retains fully explicit response columns and makes no column-generation claim. Alvarez and Ferrando's recent dynamic-regime recursion occupies rectangular chain-style backward induction but not the canonical response-width kernel. The causaloptim interface of Jonzon, Sachs, and Gabriel is the prospective consumer, contingent on a future eligible-input exporter.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The feasible response masses range over real H-polytopes; rationality is a derived property of their extreme points, not a restriction of the compatible-SCM class. The primary width bound is representation-sensitive and applies only after every canonical response coordinate, raw equality, nonnegativity record, query monomial, and decomposition bag is charged to \(B\). It does not transfer to implicit response columns or arbitrary algebraic rewrites. The secondary binary algorithm drops the width requirement but still requires the full explicit representation; its exponent depends on the number \(\ell-1\) of enumerated relevant blocks. Fixing \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is essential because optimization over a rational statistical confidence region can have irrational endpoints. A positive observed table does not justify strictly positive endpoint response masses.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proved mathematical endpoint results are distinct from executable serialized refinement. The abstract support and separator verifier is specified mathematically; the serialized parser, generator completeness proof, executable checker, adversarial corruption tests, and end-to-end refinement bit bound remain open in \(\text{oeq:executable-refinement}\). The exact endpoint and skeptical-certificate theorems apply to \(\mathfrak I_{q,k}^{\ge3}\); the one- and two-component reductions are statements over \(\mathfrak J_{q,k}\). The secondary theorem over \(\mathfrak J_2^{\mathrm{nw}}\) assumes no width bound, enumerates only \(\ell-1\) relevant-block vertex lists, and is polynomial-time when \(\ell=1\). The fully serialized fixture \(\mathsf F_\star\) fixes the graph, table, intervention, polynomial, decomposition, endpoint masses, and replay obligations. The result excludes hardness, implicit column generation, statistical projection, new elimination machinery, benchmark gains, and any claim that causaloptim already implements the fallback.

statement_notes.justification: This gives an exact second regime when no useful width decomposition is available: enumerate only all but one relevant binary block, optimize the remaining block directly, and recover a polynomial-time case when \(\ell=1\).
statement_notes.gap: Arroyo et al. obtain column generation for one intervention under a different representation; the proved logarithmic-square raw-rank bound instead yields a fully expanded exact algorithm for several relevant blocks and exposes the one-block rational-LP elbow.
statement_notes.consumer: A canonical optimizer can dispatch sparse-block binary queries even when measured scalar response width is large, using exact rational linear programming for the omitted relevant block and rational feasibility for irrelevant blocks.
